title: Towards Fair Resource Sharing in Agentic LLM Serving
content:
Computer Science > Operating Systems
  [Submitted on 17 Nov 2026]
Title:Towards Fair Resource Sharing in Agentic LLM Serving
View PDF HTML (experimental)
            Abstract:As LLM agents increasingly execute complex, multi-step tasks on shared inference infrastructure, resource contention across the end-to-end LLM serving stack causes severe and uneven slowdowns across agents. Existing agentic serving systems primarily optimize throughput and latency, with comparatively limited attention to fairness among concurrent agents. Although fairness has been studied in conventional LLM serving at the token and request levels, these approaches do not fully capture cumulative delays and stateful resource dependencies across successive LLM calls within an agent. Moreover, interference spans request routing, runtime scheduling, and hardware resources, making agent-level fairness challenging to define and optimize across an end-to-end serving stack. This paper presents a cross-layer framework to define agent-level fairness, attribute sources of unfairness, and optimize fairness while preserving throughput. To account for agents with widely varying execution demands, we build a theoretical foundation to define fairness using slowdown relative to standalone execution. Our empirical analysis reveals that routing, runtime scheduling, and hardware contention jointly determine fairness, with performance-oriented policies often leading to prolonged queuing delays. To optimize fairness, we introduce Duru, which monitors each agent's slowdown and uses this signal to guide admission and scheduling decisions across the router and runtime. Duru further alleviates starvation through admission exceptions and integrates slowdown-driven autoscaling to adhere to Service-Level Objectives (SLOs). Our evaluation across various benchmarks and hardware platforms shows that Duru reduces 99th-percentile normalized slowdown by a geometric mean of 44.4% (up to 79.5%) while delivering 91.8-127.4% of the state-of-the-art system's throughput.

report.summary: A new arXiv paper proposes a cross-layer framework and system, Duru, that defines and enforces fairness among concurrent LLM agents by tracking each agent's slowdown relative to standalone execution, cutting tail latency without sacrificing throughput.
report.background: LLM agents rarely make a single API call — they plan, call tools, retrieve context, and re-prompt the model over many steps, sometimes dozens of times per task. When many such agents share one inference cluster, they compete for the same GPUs, KV-cache memory, and request queues. Today's agentic serving stacks (routers, schedulers, autoscalers) are tuned almost entirely for aggregate throughput and average latency, so a single long-running or memory-hungry agent can inflate everyone else's completion time — a problem that gets worse as agents become the dominant inference workload. Fairness research in classical LLM serving operates at the token or single-request level, which misses the stateful, multi-call nature of an agent's execution. The paper argues that unfairness is produced jointly by request routing, runtime scheduling, and hardware contention, so any fix must span the whole stack rather than one layer.
key_points: Fairness is redefined at the agent level, not the request level: instead of counting tokens or single-call latency, the authors measure each agent's "slowdown" — how much longer its full multi-step task takes under contention versus running alone. This accommodates agents with wildly different workloads, from a quick lookup to a 50-step research task.

The authors show empirically that unfairness is cross-layer: the router's load-balancing choice, the runtime's batching and preemption policy, and raw GPU/KV-cache contention all contribute. Throughput-optimized policies often park some agents in long queues while others race ahead.

Duru, the proposed system, continuously monitors each agent's estimated slowdown and feeds that signal into both admission control (which requests enter the system) and scheduling (which run next), closing the loop between the router and the runtime.

To prevent starvation of heavy agents that would otherwise be permanently deprioritized, Duru adds admission exceptions, and it uses slowdown signals to drive autoscaling so deployments can still meet their stated service-level objectives.

Evaluated across multiple benchmarks and hardware platforms, Duru cuts 99th-percentile normalized slowdown by a geometric mean of 44.4% (up to 79.5%) while retaining 91.8–127.4% of the throughput achieved by state-of-the-art serving systems.
report.impact: For the AI industry, this shifts the conversation from raw tokens-per-second to predictability, which is what enterprises actually buy when they deploy agents. If tail latency can be tamed without throughput loss, agent platforms become viable on shared multi-tenant infrastructure rather than requiring dedicated clusters per customer. For developers, the paper's key lesson is architectural: fairness cannot be patched into a scheduler alone, because routing decisions upstream can doom an agent before it ever reaches the GPU. That implies instrumenting agent-level slowdown as a first-class metric alongside latency and QPS. For regular users, the practical effect is fewer pathological waits — an agent that usually answers in 20 seconds shouldn't occasionally take five minutes because another tenant launched a batch job. The caveat: the gains come from a research prototype, and production systems will need to adopt similar monitoring before the benefit is real.
report.tools: To follow up, read the paper on arXiv (2611.23558) and compare it with open-source serving stacks where these ideas would land: vLLM and SGLang (scheduling, continuous batching, KV-cache management), llm-d and the Gateway API Inference Extension (agent-aware routing), AIBrix and Ray Serve (multi-tenant model serving), plus DistServe for goodput-oriented scheduling. For implementing slowdown-based autoscaling, pair Prometheus and Grafana metrics with KEDA or Kubernetes HPA.
